a: Is it allowed to heal on the Sabbath, or not?
p: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus lack "or not" and phrase the question differently (KJV "Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath day?").

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and THGNT (manuscripts not checked here)
readings.orig: Ἔξεστιν τῷ σαββάτῳ θεραπεῦσαι ἢ οὔ;
readings.en: Is it permitted on the Sabbath to heal, or not?
readings.plain: Is it allowed to heal on the Sabbath, or not?

readings.w: The Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and the Textus Receptus (KJV); manuscripts not checked here
readings.en: Is it permitted on the Sabbath to heal?
readings.plain: Is it allowed to heal on the Sabbath?

why: The critical editions print "or not"; the shorter question may have been shaped by the parallel in Matthew 12:10. The meaning is the same either way.

t: A son, a donkey or a sheep?
p: The oldest papyri say "a son or an ox". Other manuscripts say "a donkey or an ox" (KJV) or "a sheep or an ox".

readings.w: P45 (200s), P75 (about 175–225), Codex Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), Washington (W) and the Byzantine majority (as reported by Metzger); SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
Codex Sinaiticus (01), L, Ψ, families 1 and 13 and others (as reported by Metzger); the Textus Receptus (KJV "an ass or an ox")
Codex Bezae (05) (as reported by Metzger)

why: "A son or an ox" is the oldest reading and the harder one: a child and an animal make an odd pair, so copyists changed "son" to "donkey" to match the ox and donkey of 13:15 (and Deuteronomy 22:4), or to "sheep" to match Matthew 12:11. No copyist would have changed "donkey" to "son".

p: The Byzantine text has the guest say "dinner" (ἄριστον) instead of "bread" (ἄρτον).

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles; the Textus Receptus (KJV "eat bread")
The Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont)

why: The two Greek words differ by two letters. "Eat bread" is the Jewish idiom for sharing a meal and is in the oldest manuscripts; "dinner" picks up the word used in 14:12.

p: The KJV's "for all things are now ready" follows later manuscripts that add "all things".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
The Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: because all things are ready now

why: The shorter text is in the older manuscripts that the critical editions follow; "all things" is a natural addition that does not change the sense.

p: The Byzantine text ends the parable with Matthew's line, "For the called are many, but the chosen are few."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles; the Textus Receptus (KJV)
The Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and many later manuscripts
readings.orig: γεύσεταί μου τοῦ δείπνου. πολλοὶ γάρ εἰσιν κλητοί, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοί.
readings.en: will taste my dinner. For many are called, but few chosen.
readings.plain: will taste my supper. For the called are many, but the chosen are few.

why: The line belongs to Matthew's wedding parable (Matthew 22:14) and to some manuscripts of Matthew 20:16. Copyists who knew Matthew's version added it here. It is absent from the older manuscripts and even from the Textus Receptus, so the KJV does not have it.

p: The oldest manuscripts say he longed "to be fed". The SBLGNT and later manuscripts have the blunter "to fill his belly" (KJV).

readings.w: P75, Codex Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), Bezae (05), L and family 1 (as reported by Metzger); NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: to be fed with, to eat his fill from

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (02), Θ, Ψ, family 13 and the Byzantine majority; the Textus Receptus (KJV "fain have filled his belly with"); SBLGNT

why: Here the Plain follows NA28 and the Tyndale House edition against the SBLGNT. "Eat his fill" has the oldest and widest early support, including P75 and Vaticanus. The SBLGNT prints the cruder "fill his belly," and a case can be made for it: copyists may have refined a vulgar phrase, and "eat his fill" could have come in from 16:21, where Lazarus longs to eat his fill. The early evidence decides it here.
b: The difference is one of tone, not meaning: in both readings the son is starving and wants what the pigs eat.

a: I don't deserve to be called your son anymore.
t: Did the son finish his speech?
p: Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and Bezae add "Make me like one of your hired men", completing the speech the son had planned.

readings.w: P75, Codex Alexandrinus (02), L, W, Θ, Ψ, families 1 and 13, the Byzantine majority (as reported by Metzger); SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT; the Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: οὐκέτι εἰμὶ ἄξιος κληθῆναι υἱός σου.
readings.en: I am no longer worthy to be called your son.
readings.plain: I don't deserve to be called your son anymore.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), Bezae (05), 33 and a few others (as reported by Metzger); printed by Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: οὐκέτι εἰμὶ ἄξιος κληθῆναι υἱός σου· ποίησόν με ὡς ἕνα τῶν μισθίων σου.
readings.en: I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired men.
readings.plain: I don't deserve to be called your son anymore. Make me like one of your hired men.

why: Copyists naturally completed the speech from 15:19. Without the last line, the story has its point: the father interrupts before the son can ask to be made a hired man. The shorter text is supported by P75 and a broad range of witnesses, so even though Sinaiticus and Vaticanus agree on the longer one, nearly all editors judge it an assimilation.

a: Hurry, bring out a robe, the best one
p: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus lack "Hurry" (KJV "Bring forth the best robe").

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and THGNT (manuscripts not checked here)
readings.en: Quickly bring out a robe, the first one
readings.plain: Hurry, bring out a robe, the best one

readings.w: The Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and the Textus Receptus (KJV); manuscripts not checked here

why: The critical editions print ταχύ. The word adds urgency to the father's orders but does not change the story.

p: The KJV's "when ye fail" follows the later reading. The older one says "when it [the wealth] runs out".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
The Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus (KJV "when ye fail")

why: The singular, with wealth as its subject, is the reading of the older manuscripts. The plural, "when you fail," means "when you die" and may have been suggested by the following "they will take you." The sense is close: money will not outlast this life.

p: Codex Vaticanus and L read "what is ours", which Westcott and Hort printed.

readings.w: Most manuscripts, including Codex Sinaiticus (01) and Alexandrinus (02) (as reported in NA28); SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Tregelles; the Textus Receptus (KJV "that which is your own")
Codex Vaticanus (03) and L, with Origen (as reported in NA28); Westcott-Hort

why: "Yours" has the widest support and makes the contrast with "what belongs to another" clear. In later Greek ἡμέτερον and ὑμέτερον sounded nearly the same, so copyists confused them often. "Ours" would mean the true riches belonging to God and Jesus, which they share with disciples, an attractive sense that made Westcott and Hort prefer it.

t: A name for the rich man
p: The oldest manuscript of Luke, P75, gives the rich man a name: Neues.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT; the Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: there was a certain rich man

readings.w: P75 (about 175–225); compare the Sahidic Coptic, which names him Nineveh (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: Ἄνθρωπος δέ τις ἦν πλούσιος ὀνόματι Νευης
readings.en: there was a certain rich man named Neues
readings.plain: A certain man was rich, and his name was Neues.

why: The parable names only the poor man. Later readers wanted a name for the rich man too, and different traditions supplied different ones; P75's "Neues" may be a shortened form of the Coptic "Nineveh." Latin readers came to call him Dives, which is simply the Latin word for "rich man."

p: The KJV's "crumbs" comes from later manuscripts, which add the word from Matthew 15:27.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
The Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus (KJV "with the crumbs which fell")
readings.plain: from the scraps that dropped off

why: The older manuscripts lack the noun. Copyists added it from the Canaanite woman's reply, "the little dogs do eat some of the scraps that drop from their owners' table" (Matthew 15:27), a natural association since dogs appear in both scenes.

t: A millstone, or a donkey's millstone?
p: Later manuscripts of Luke have Matthew's and Mark's "donkey's millstone".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
The Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus (KJV "a millstone")

why: The older text has Luke's own phrase; copyists brought it into line with Matthew 18:6 and Mark 9:42. The KJV's "a millstone" does not show the difference.

p: The KJV's "if thy brother trespass against thee" follows later manuscripts that add "against you".

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
The Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἐὰν δὲ ἁμάρτῃ εἰς σὲ ὁ ἀδελφός σου
readings.en: if your brother sins against you
readings.plain: If your brother sins against you

why: The addition comes from the next verse ("sins against you") and from Matthew 18:15. Without it, the saying covers any sin of a fellow believer, not only a personal wrong; the older manuscripts lack it.

p: The KJV's "I trow not" translates two words found only in later manuscripts.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.orig: μὴ ἔχει χάριν τῷ δούλῳ ὅτι ἐποίησεν τὰ διαταχθέντα;
readings.en: he does not thank the slave because he did what was ordered, does he?

readings.w: The Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus (KJV "I trow not")
readings.en: ... what was ordered him? I think not.
readings.plain: does he? I don't think so.

why: The question already expects the answer "no," and "I think not" spells it out. The words are missing from the older manuscripts and look like an explanatory addition.

a: through the country between Samaria and Galilee
t: Between, or through the middle of?
p: The critical editions read διὰ μέσον, "between"; the Byzantine text has διὰ μέσου, "through the middle of" (KJV "through the midst of Samaria and Galilee").

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 and THGNT (manuscripts not checked here)
readings.plain: through the country between Samaria and Galilee

readings.w: The Byzantine majority text (Robinson-Pierpont) and the Textus Receptus (KJV); manuscripts not checked here
readings.en: through the middle of Samaria and Galilee
readings.plain: through the middle of Samaria and Galilee

why: Διὰ μέσον (accusative) is the unusual form and the one the critical editions print; διὰ μέσου (genitive) is the ordinary Greek for "through the midst of" and may be a copyist's smoothing. The difference matters for the route: "between" suggests a road along the border (see the note).

p: P75, Vaticanus and Bezae lack "in his day". NA28 prints it in brackets.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), L, W, Θ, Ψ and most manuscripts (as reported by Metzger); SBLGNT, NA28 (in brackets), THGNT, Tregelles; the Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: οὕτως ἔσται ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ αὐτοῦ
readings.en: so will the Son of Man be in his day

readings.w: P75, Codex Vaticanus (03), Bezae (05) and some Old Latin manuscripts (as reported by Metzger); Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: οὕτως ἔσται ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
readings.en: so will the Son of Man be

why: The witnesses are evenly balanced. The words might have dropped out by accident, the eye skipping from one ending to another, or have been added to match "the days of the Son of Man" around them. Most editions keep them, with NA28 marking its doubt by brackets. The sense hardly changes.

a: tries to hold on to his life
p: The KJV's "seek to save his life" follows the later wording, which matches 9:24.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT, Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.en: seeks to keep his life safe
readings.plain: tries to hold on to his life

readings.w: The Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: Luke's rare verb was replaced by the usual "save" of the other forms of this saying (9:24; Mark 8:35). The older manuscripts keep the rarer word.

a: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]
p: A verse added from Matthew 24:40. It is in the KJV, but not in the oldest manuscripts or most later ones.

readings.w: P75, Codex Sinaiticus (01), Alexandrinus (02), Vaticanus (03), L, W, Θ, Ψ, family 1 and the Byzantine majority (as reported by Metzger); SBLGNT, NA28, THGNT
readings.plain: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]

readings.w: Codex Bezae (05), family 13, 700, most Old Latin manuscripts, the Vulgate and the Syriac versions (as reported by Metzger); the Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: δύο ἐν ἀγρῷ· εἷς παραλημφθήσεται καὶ ὁ ἕτερος ἀφεθήσεται
readings.en: Two in the field: one will be taken and the other will be left.
readings.plain: There will be two men out in a field. One will be taken along, and the other will be left behind.

why: The verse is missing from nearly all Greek manuscripts, old and late. It was added in the West to complete the pattern of Matthew 24:40 (two in the field, two at the mill); in Luke the pair is two in a bed and two at the mill. Copying it in was easy, since it ends like 17:35. It came into the printed Textus Receptus and so into the KJV, though most Greek manuscripts, including the Byzantine majority, lack it. The Greek given here is the TR's text as listed in the STEPBible word list.
